Spatial distribution, ecological risk, and source apportionment of sedimentary metals in the Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem of Bangladesh

What do sediment-metal measurements reveal about contamination, ecological risk and potential source processes in the Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem?

Md. Shohel Parvez · Sajib Roy · Md. Robin Ahmed · Afif Iftikhar · Md. Hasib Mahmudul Haque Rumi · Sadhon Chandra Swarnokar · Rahat Khan

Bangladesh SundarbansSediment geochemistryMarine Pollution Bulletin · Vol. 232Article 120042

Scientific focus

Research question & objectives

Mangrove sediments store metals carried by riverine, tidal and human-related processes. This study examined both the observed sediment chemistry and the evidence for potential controls on that chemistry.

How are metals distributed across sampled Sundarbans sediments, how do contamination and potential ecological-risk indices vary, and which geochemical processes best explain the measured patterns?

Objective 1

Measure spatial patterns

Quantify the concentrations of 16 elements and examine differences among sampling locations.

Objective 2

Evaluate contamination and risk

Use sediment-quality comparisons and complementary contamination and ecological-risk indices.

Objective 3

Interpret potential sources

Combine correlation, principal components, clustering and positive matrix factorization to interpret co-varying element groups.

Geographical context

Sampling across the Sundarbans

Twenty-two surface-sediment samples were collected across the Khulna, Chandpai and Sarankhola ranges of the Bangladesh Sundarbans. The spatial analysis used these point measurements, not a continuous map of sediment contamination.

How the study was conducted

From sediment samples to source interpretation

The analysis linked laboratory measurements with standardized indices and multivariate models. The methods address related but distinct questions: how much metal was present, how that compares with reference values, and which patterns may share common controls.

01 · Field and laboratory

Sampling & measurements

Surface sediments, approximately 5–10 cm depth, were prepared for instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA) and atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS). Quality checks used certified reference materials and replicate measurements.

02 · Contamination & risk

Multiple screening indices

Contamination factor (CF), enrichment factor (EF), geo-accumulation (Igeo), pollution load index (PLI), and potential ecological risk index (PERI) were calculated from elemental measurements and reference values.

03 · Interpretation

Spatial and source patterns

Sample-location maps, Pearson correlations, PCA, hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) and positive matrix factorization (PMF) were used to compare the patterns of elements and infer possible controlling processes.

Important distinction: a concentration map shows an observation; a contamination or risk index interprets it relative to a reference; and a PMF factor is a statistical interpretation of a shared chemical signature. These are different levels of evidence.

Result 1 · Elemental distribution

Spatial patterns were not uniform

Measured elements showed contrasting spatial signatures. Several major lithogenic elements, including Al, K, Sc and V, had relatively consistent patterns, whereas Zn, Pb, As and Hg exhibited more spatially localized elevations. The maps do not by themselves establish what caused those elevations.

Broad geochemical background

Conservative mineral-associated elements were consistent with natural sediment supply, weathering and estuarine sorting.

Localized enrichment

Some trace-element patterns were consistent with mixtures of natural sediment processes and human-associated inputs, rather than a uniform corridor-wide hotspot.

Result 2 · Contamination status

Mostly limited enrichment, with local departures

The contamination measures largely indicated low to moderate relative contamination. Most CF values were below 2, and enrichment factors were generally near or below 1.5; some sampled locations showed higher relative values for Zn, Pb, As and related elements. Each index relies on comparison with a selected background composition.

How to read these results: the heatmaps and distributions are chemical screening evidence. They do not directly measure ecological injury, metal uptake by organisms, or human exposure.

Result 3 · Ecological-risk indices

Overall risk classification was low; individual metals still mattered

The aggregate potential ecological risk index (PERI) placed all 22 sites in the study’s low-risk category, while pollution load index (PLI) values remained below 1. However, Hg and As contributed disproportionately to the modeled metal-specific risk. A low aggregate index should therefore not be read as proof of ecological safety.

Hg & AsParticularly important to element-specific potential-risk interpretation

Indices depend on toxicity factors, background reference values and the sampled locations. They are not direct measurements of biological effects or food-chain transfer.

Result 4 · Geochemical source patterns

Four interpretable source-related factors

Multivariate analysis showed that metals tended to group in ways consistent with mineral composition, detrital inputs and geochemical transformations, alongside a component associated with anthropogenic enrichment. PCA and HCA support similarities among elements and sites, while PMF models the underlying factor profiles.

Factor 1

Estuarine lithogenic matrix

Associated with major mineral and estuarine sediment components, including Na, Ca and Al.

Factor 2

Terrigenous detrital inputs

A signature consistent with weathering-derived and river-transported material, including Sc, Al, Cr, K and V.

Factor 3

Secondary geochemical enrichment

Fe- and Mn-associated patterns consistent with reactive mineral phases and changing redox conditions.

Factor 4

Anthropogenic enrichment

A factor marked by Hg, Pb and As, interpreted as reflecting potential human-related inputs superimposed on the natural sediment background.

Model interpretation: PMF identifies statistical factors in the sampled chemistry. It does not directly measure individual industries’ emissions, identify a unique discharge point, or establish causal sources without independent source measurements.

Scientific interpretation

What the combined evidence tells us

Taken together, the observed sediment chemistry and the index- and model-based analyses indicate a predominantly natural geochemical background, overlaid with localized enrichment of selected metals and possible anthropogenic contributions.

Background processes dominate

Riverborne mineral material, tidal sorting and sediment geochemistry explain much of the multielement structure.

Aggregate indices need context

Low overall PERI and PLI values do not remove the importance of potentially toxic elements at individual sites.

Monitoring should be targeted

Hg, As and Pb deserve continued attention, especially where shipping, urban runoff and other pressures may affect sediment quality.

Boundaries of the evidence

  • Sampling coverage: 22 surface-sediment samples provide a spatial snapshot, not a time series or a complete characterization of every Sundarbans channel.
  • Risk interpretation: the calculated indices are screening indicators; biological exposure, speciation, bioavailability and toxicity were not directly measured by this study.
  • Source inference: factor analysis separates correlated signatures but cannot by itself distinguish all possible natural versus human sources or demonstrate causality.
